The Frog Guiro (güiro) is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.23. The body is usually a gourd, hollow and open at one end, and it is also made from other fruits, wood, synthetic fibre or metal; the surface is cut with parallel ridges and usually drilled with fingerholes so the fingers can hold it. The player scrapes a short wooden stick or a toothed scraper back and forth along the ridges, making a ratchet sound like a zip. It is common in the music of Cuba, Puerto Rico and other parts of Latin America, usually played by the singer or by the rhythm section, at traditional dances, religious festivals and dance performances, and it is an important rhythm instrument in Colombian cumbia as well.
刮瓜屬體鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 112.23，常見於加勒: The güiro is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.23, common in Caribbean and Latin American music. The body is hollow, open at one end and drilled with fingerholes; the player puts the fingers into the holes to hold it, and the surface is cut with parallel ridges. To begin, use a short wooden stick or a metal scraper and rub back and forth along the ridges, making sound by friction; practise long and short scrapes first, with up and down directions, to make continuous and broken rhythms.
刮瓜常見於古巴、波多黎各與拉丁美洲音樂，在頌樂、特羅瓦、騷莎的節奏組中擔任刮擦聲: The güiro is common in the music of Cuba, Puerto Rico and Latin America; it takes the scraping part in the rhythm sections of son, trova and salsa, and it is also used in the traditional dance and festival line-ups of danzón, plena, seis, danza, cumbia and mejorana, often played by the singer at the same time. In classical and orchestral music it is used in Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, Morton Gould's Latin American Symphonette, Villa-Lobos's Uirapuru (whose score calls for a reco-reco) and Shchedrin's Carmen Suite, the ballet arranged from Bizet's opera; American rock songs also feature the güiro rhythm.
刮瓜起源說法不一。有資料稱源自波多黎各，另有資料指其由南美樂器演變：阿茲特克人以: Accounts of the güiro's origin differ. One source says it comes from Puerto Rico, another that it developed from South American instruments: the Aztecs made scrapers from small serrated bones, and the Taíno of the Caribbean developed the ridged long gourd or animal-bone scraper that is the modern predecessor. A third account points to African scrapers, connecting it with scraping idiophones in Cameroon and in West and Central Africa. In making, the dried gourd gave way to wood, synthetic fibre and metal.

青蛙刮鼓具有獨特的明亮而富有穿透力的音色，帶有幽默詼諧的質感。其音域集中在中高頻: The frog guiro has a distinctive bright, penetrating timbre with a humorous, comic quality. Its range sits in the upper middle frequencies and it makes a crisp, sharp scraping sound, like a real frog croaking. Playing rubs the scraper back and forth over the frog's back, setting the wooden resonance chamber vibrating and producing a warm, resonant sound. Against the clear separate notes of the traditional xylophone the frog guiro has a rougher, grainier texture; against the shaker its timbre is sharper and stronger. Because it imitates a natural sound, it is often used to create atmosphere and a sense of rhythm, and it is widely used in children's music and percussion ensembles in particular.

Traditionally it is made from a dried gourd, its surface cut with parallel ridges; modern ones are also made of wood, glass fibre or synthetic fibre. It is played by scraping back and forth with a short wooden stick, and there is also a metal variant, ridged on the outside and rubbed with a metal scraper or stick, sealed inside and filled with iron sand.
